answer.exemplar: A timer is a bet on a path, and no document can know the path. On a wide link a segment is acknowledged in microseconds, so a 200-millisecond wait means the retransmission goes out long after the original has been received, and the sender has thrown away good throughput to protect a network that was never in trouble. On a narrow or distant path the same 200 milliseconds can be shorter than a single round trip, so the timer expires before the first acknowledgement could possibly have returned and the sender floods the link with copies of data that is still on its way. The two failures have opposite signs, and a fixed value produces one of them on every path. What a sender should do instead is measure the round trip continuously, keep an estimate with some margin, and raise that estimate when a retransmission turns out to have been unnecessary, because that is evidence the first estimate was too small. The cost of measuring is a little state per connection and a little arithmetic. The cost of not measuring is that one constant behaves correctly on the test network and badly everywhere else.

questions.explanation: A fixed timer is a statement about a path the writer never measured, and the error it makes has two opposite signs: on a short path it retransmits data that has already arrived, and on a long path it retransmits before the first copy could have been acknowledged. questions.explanation: Reliability is a claim about loss and order and nothing else: the bytes the sender hands over arrive at the peer, in the sequence they were given, with any hole filled by resending. answer.exemplar: Ordering and delivery are the same property here, and they pull against each other. A stream hands bytes to the program in one sequence, so a program that reads 8, 9 and 10 has already been told that 7 exists and is coming, and delivering those three out of order would make the program's own data wrong. The receiver is therefore holding three perfectly good pieces of data in a buffer it cannot use, and the sender has three acknowledged pieces of window it cannot reclaim, because the acknowledgement for them is stuck behind the gap. The cost is not the lost segment, which is one segment. It is that the transfer's progress is governed by the slowest moment on the whole path rather than by the average, and a path with a burst of loss turns a fast link into one whose effective rate is set by the worst gap in it. A connectionless transport has no such coupling, which is why it is the right choice when a gap costs one frame of audio and the wrong choice when it would desynchronise a file.

questions.stem: A service must accept an order and then do work that takes four seconds. Which arrangement should it use, and what does that choice move onto the caller and its handler?
questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Direct call against a message for slow work

answer.exemplar: The two arrangements fail in different places, which is the reason to choose between them rather than to combine them blindly. A direct call puts the failure inside the user's request: the caller holds a thread, its reply time is the sum of its own work and the dependency's, and when the dependency is slow the user waits and when it is down the user is refused. Nothing about that failure is hidden from the user, and that is the useful property, because the person who made the request is present for the answer. A message moves the work behind the reply, and the failure then surfaces at the consumer instead, minutes or hours from the request and with no user attached to it. What the message hides is the outcome: acceptance is the only thing the reply can mean, and the work may still fail, be retried, or arrive twice. The honest reading of the second arrangement is therefore that it trades a visible failure for a hidden one, and buys a service that stays up while its dependencies do not.

questions.explanation: A direct call makes the dependency's failure the user's failure, in the same request and in front of the same person. A message moves that failure to the consumer, where it appears long after the reply and with nobody waiting, so the arrangement hides the outcome rather than removing it. The trade is a visible failure for a hidden one, and the price is availability bought at the cost of certainty.
questions.hint: Ask where each failure surfaces, and who is present when it does.

questions.explanation: A breaker exists to stop a caller spending its own workers and connections on a dependency that is failing, so the measure has to be about that call's outcomes: a run of consecutive failures, or a failure rate over a window, sometimes with slow calls counted as failures. Whatever it counts, the calls are still made, so the cost is a small number of doomed calls per window, and that is the price of not drawing the conclusion from one unlucky request. A queue length describes the dependency's load rather than this caller's results, and an average reply time describes its history: both are dominated by other traffic and both can look healthy while this caller fails steadily. A total call count rises on a good day too, and rises faster the more successful the dependency is, so it measures popularity rather than health.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence the caller's own experience provides, rather than what the dependency looks like from outside.

questions.explanation: The order is forced by what each state is for. A closed breaker is no breaker at all: calls pass straight through and the failures are counted as a by-product of doing the work, which is the only way to know whether the dependency is failing. The count is what decides the transition, and once the measure is crossed the breaker opens, where its whole purpose is to refuse immediately so the dependency is not kept under load by callers who cannot be helped. After a wait, and not before, a small number of trial calls are let through, because the caller has no way to know the dependency is healthy again except by trying it. Whether those trials succeed decides the last step: success closes the breaker and traffic returns to normal, and a single failure among them reopens it for another full wait, which is why the trial number is kept small.
questions.hint: Ask what each state is for, and what evidence moves it to the next one.

questions.explanation: A bulkhead is a separate, separately sized pool per dependency, so a failure consumes only the resource that dependency's calls use. With one pool per dependency, all 40 workers waiting on the hung call are workers the other two dependencies would have used, and the other two pools stay available for the traffic that does not touch the failing call. B leaves the fault in place, because a shared pool between two dependencies can still be emptied by the third one's behaviour through the callers that reach it. C multiplies the resource without partitioning it, so the same proportion of a larger pool is consumed and free workers still reach zero. D spreads the dependency across workers rather than isolating it, and a hung call holds whichever worker it landed on. The cost is workers and connections held in reserve rather than doing work, which is the price of being able to serve the rest.

questions.explanation: Order within one account is only meaningful along that account's own sequence, so every update for an account has to reach a single consumer that sees them all, which is what routing on the account identifier achieves. Everything about the cost follows from that: the consumer for an account is one work unit, so an account producing a high rate of updates becomes a hot partition and a ceiling on its own throughput even while spare capacity sits on other partitions. Adding consumers does not relieve that ceiling unless the key is spread, and spreading it costs the ordering that was just bought. One queue with many consumers gives the order up the moment a second consumer exists. Routing by the bank pools every account onto one consumer, which is a coarser key than the requirement. Sorting by the sender's clock restores nothing, because a clock is not the order it sent in.

questions.explanation: The fixed window counts against the clock, and the two bursts fall into two different windows: 100 in each is within the limit of 100 a second, so all 200 are accepted and the client really did make 200 calls in 0.2 seconds, which is 1,000 a second. The bucket has a physical quantity of credit with a capacity of 100, so it is empty after the first burst and 10 more arrive over the next tenth of a second: 110 served, 90 waiting. The two policies therefore differ in what they bound, and the difference only shows at a boundary or a spike. Calling either one compliant by averaging is the arithmetic slip, since an average over the whole second of 100 a second is compatible with an instant rate of 1,000 and protects nothing at the instant it matters.

answer.exemplar: Three layers each contribute something, and the outage is what happens when they are all tuned to hide their own limits. The queue is the first: it absorbs the difference between a steady arrival rate and a slower consumer, and while it absorbs it the work is not lost, only late. But a queue is also a delay amplifier, because a consumer that is persistently behind never catches up on its own, so every second of arrival at 40 and retirement at less than 40 adds a second of waiting to everything already inside, and the callers see that waiting grow before they see any error. The dependency supplies the second contribution, since a call that takes twenty seconds is twenty seconds of a consumer held hostage, and the caller behind it cannot tell a slow call from a lost one. The single consumer per account is the third, and it is the reason a busy account cannot borrow capacity from a quiet one. The change that breaks the chain is to make the consumer's rate visible and enforced at the boundary: cap what is taken per account so depth cannot grow without limit, and every other fix then has a limit to sit inside.

questions.explanation: The queue converts a rate difference into growing delay before it produces any error, the slow dependency converts into held consumers, and the per-account consumer stops capacity being borrowed across accounts. The chain breaks where the growth is made visible and bounded, which is at the entry to the queue rather than at the exit from it.
questions.hint: Ask which layer converts a small rate difference into a visible failure, and where that growth can be stopped.
